waiver — granted before the financial statements were 
approved for issue — of a breach of a material covenant in 
a long term loan arrangement that occurred on or before 
the end of the reporting period, resulting in the liability 
becoming payable on demand at the reporting date, was 
regarded as an adjusting event.
 For annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1st 
April 2026, any breach of a covenant — whether material 
or immaterial — occurring on or before the reporting 
date will, in accordance with Ind AS 1, require the related 
liability to be classified as current, unless the lender has 
granted a waiver of the breach on or before the reporting 
date and has agreed not to demand repayment for at least 
12 months after the reporting date as a consequence of the 
breach. Such a waiver shall be treated as an adjusting event.
 The amendments are effective for annual reporting periods 
beginning on or after 1st April 2026 retrospectively in 
accordance with Ind AS 8.
 The Group has no impact of these amendments in its 
classification criteria of current and non-current liabilities.
2.30 New and amended standards
 The Group applied for the first-time certain standards 
and amendments, which are effective for annual periods 
beginning on or after 1st April, 2025. The Group has not 
early adopted any standard, interpretation or amendment 
that has been issued but is not yet effective.
 (i) Amendments to Ind AS 21 - Lack of exchangeability
  The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) vide 
notification dated 7th May 2025, notified the Companies 
(Indian Accounting Standards) Amendment Rules, 
2025, which amend Ind AS 21, The Effects of Changes 
in Foreign Exchange Rates to specify how an entity 
should assess whether a currency is exchangeable 
and how it should determine a spot exchange rate 
when exchangeability is lacking. The amendments 
also require disclosure of information that enables 
users of its financial statements to understand 
how the currency not being exchangeable into the 
other currency affects, or is expected to affect, the 
entity’s financial performance, financial position 
and cash flows.  The amendments are effective for annual reporting 
periods beginning on or after 1st April, 2025. When 
applying the amendments, an entity cannot restate 
comparative information. 
  The amendments do not have a material impact on 
the Group’s consolidated financial statements.
(ii) Amendments to Ind AS 1 - Classification of 
Liabilities as Current or Non-current and Non-
current Liabilities with Covenants
  The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) vide  
notification dated 13th August 2025, notified  
amendments to paragraphs 69 to 76 of Ind AS  
1 Presentation of Financial Statements to specify the 
requirements for classifying liabilities as current or 
non-current. The amendment relates to classification 
of liabilities as current or non-current and clarifies that 
covenants that affects the classification of a liability as 
current or non-current must exist at the reporting date 
and have substance. The amendment also introduces 
guidance on classification of liabilities with covenants. 
  The amendments are effective for annual reporting 
periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025 
retrospectively in accordance with Ind AS 8.
  The Group has no impact of these amendments 
in its classification criteria of current and non-
current liabilities. 
(iii) Amendments to Ind AS 7 and Ind AS 107 – Supplier 
Finance Arrangements
  The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) vide 
notification dated 13th August 2025, notified the 
amendment in Ind AS 7 Statement of Cash Flows 
requires an entity to disclose information about 
supplier financing arrangements and explain the 
nature of the arrangements, the carrying amount of 
liabilities and the range of payment due dates. Ind 
AS 107 Financial Instruments: Disclosures has been 
amended to add supplier financing arrangements as 
a factor that may cause concentration of liquidity risk. 
  The Group has reviewed the amendment and based 
on its evaluation has determined that it does not have 
any impact in its consolidated financial statements. 
The amendments are effective for annual reporting 
periods beginning on or after 1st April 2025.

(i) Securities premium: Securities premium is used to record the premium on issue of shares. The reserve can be utilised only for 
limited purposes such as issuance of bonus shares in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
(ii) Capital reserve: The Group recognises profit or loss on purchase, sale, issue or cancellation of the Group’s own equity instruments 
to capital reserve.
(iii) General Reserve: General reserve was created through an annual transfer of net income at a specified percentage in accordance 
with applicable regulations under the erstwhile Companies Act, 1956. Consequent to introduction of Companies Act, 2013, the 
requirement to mandatorily transfer a specified percentage of the net profit to general reserve has been withdrawn.
(iv) Retained earnings are the profits/(loss) that the Group has earned/incurred till date, less any transfers to general reserve, 
dividends or other distributions paid to shareholders. Retained earnings include re-measurement loss/(gain) on defined benefit 
plans, net of taxes that will not be reclassified to Statement of Profit and Loss.
(v) Foreign currency translation reserve: Exchange differences arising on translation of the foreign operations are recognised 
in other comprehensive income as described in accounting policy and accumulated in a separate reserve within equity. The 
cumulative amount is reclassified to profit or loss when the net investment is disposed-off.
(vi) Cash flow hedging reserve: The Group uses hedging instruments as part of its management of commodity risks and interest rate 
risks (refer note 32). For hedging commodity risks and interest rate risk, the Group uses commodity swaps, interest rate swaps 
and interest rate caps. To the extent these hedges are effective, the change in fair value of the hedging instrument is recognised 
in the effective portion of cash flow hedges. Amounts recognised in the effective portion of cash flow hedges is reclassified to 
the statement of profit and loss when the hedged item affects profit or loss.
(vii) Reserve for equity instruments through other comprehensive income: The Group has elected to recognise changes in the fair 
value of certain investments in equity securities in other comprehensive income. These changes are accumulated within the 
Equity instruments through Other Comprehensive Income Reserve within equity. The Group may transfer amounts from this 
reserve to retained earnings when the relevant equity securities are derecognised.

Notes forming part of the Consolidated Financial Statements The management assessed that the fair values of short term financial assets and liabilities approximate their carrying amounts 
largely due to the short - term maturities of these instruments. The fair value of the financial assets and liabilities is included at 
the amount at which the instrument could be exchanged in a current transaction between willing parties, other than in a forced 
or liquidation sale.
 The Group determines fair values of financial assets and financial liabilities by discounting the contractual cash inflows/outflows 
using prevailing interest rates of financials instruments with similar terms. The initial measurement of financial assets and financial 
liabilities is at fair value except trade receivables. The fair value of investment is determined using quoted net assets value from 
the fund/share market prices. Further, the subsequent measurement of all financial assets and liabilities (other than investment 
in mutual funds, equity shares and foreign currency derivatives) is at amortised cost, using the effective interest method.
 Discount rates used in determining fair value 
 The interest rate used to discount estimated future cash flows, where applicable, are based on the incremental borrowing rate 
of the borrower which in case of financial liabilities is the weighted average cost of borrowing of the respective entity and in case 
of financial assets is the average market rate of similar credit rated instrument.
 The Group maintains policies and procedures to value financial assets or financial liabilities using the best and most relevant 
data available. In addition, the Group internally reviews valuation, including independent price validation for certain instruments. 
 Fair value of financial assets and liabilities is the amount that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an 
orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date, regardless of whether that price is directly observable 
or estimated using another valuation technique.
 The following methods and assumptions were used to estimate fair value:
 (a) Fair value of short term financial assets and liabilities approximate their carrying amounts largely due to the short term 
maturities of these instruments.
 (b) Fair value of quoted mutual funds is based on the net assets value at the reporting date. The fair value of other financial 
liabilities as well as other non current financial liabilities is estimated by discounting future cash flow using rate currently 
applicable for debt on similar terms, credit risk and remaining maturities.
 (c) The fair value of the Group’s interest bearing borrowing received are determined using discount rate that reflects the 
entity's borrowing rate as at the end of the reporting period. The own non performance risk as at the reporting was 
assessed to be insignificant.
 (d) For method and computation of deferred payment liability refer note 26(b).
 Fair Value Hierarchy
 All financial instruments for which fair value is recognised or disclosed are categorised within the fair value hierarchy described 
as follows, based on the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement as a whole:
 Level 1: Quoted (unadjusted) price in active market for identical assets or liabilities 
 Level 2: This level of hierarchy includes financial assets, measured using inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1 
that are observable for the asset, either directly (i.e., as prices) or indirectly (i.e., derived from prices).
 Level 3: Valuation technique for which the lowest level input has a significant effect on the fair value measurement is not based 
on observable market data

and 31st March, 2025:

32 Financial Instruments and Risk Review
I) Capital Management
 The Group’s capital management objectives are:
 The Board policy is to maintain a strong capital base so as to maintain investor, creditor and market confidence and to sustain 
future development of the business. The Board of Directors monitors the return on capital employed on a quarterly basis.
 The Group manages capital risk by maintaining sound/optimal capital structure through monitoring of financial ratios, such as 
debt-to-equity ratio and net borrowings-to-equity ratio on a quarterly basis and implements capital structure improvement plan 
when necessary. 
 The Group uses debt ratio as a capital management index and calculates the ratio as net debt divided by total equity. Net debt 
and total equity are based on the amounts stated in the consolidated financial statements.
 Debt-to-equity ratio is as follows:

II) Financial Risk Management Framework
 The Group is exposed primarily to market risk (fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rate), credit risk, 
liquidity risk, which may adversely impact the fair value of its financial instruments. The Group assesses the unpredictability of 
the financial environment and seeks to mitigate potential adverse effects on the financial performance of the Group.
 i) Credit Risk
  Credit risk is the risk of financial loss arising from counterparty failure to repay or service debt according to contractual 
terms. Credit risk encompasses, the risk of default, the risk of deterioration of creditworthiness of the counterparty as well 
as concentration of risks.
  Financial instruments that are subject to exposure to credit risk consist of trade receivables, investments and other 
financial assets.
264  
|Endurance Technologies Limited
=== page 253 ===
Notes forming part of the Consolidated Financial Statements  Credit risk is the risk that a counterparty will not meet its obligations under a financial instrument or customer contract, 
leading to a financial loss. The Group is exposed to credit risk from operating activities, primarily from trade receivables.
  Trade receivables
  Trade receivables consist of receivables arising primarily due to sale of goods.  These receivables are unsecured and are 
payable at the end of a specified credit period depending upon the terms of contract of each customer, which ranges from 
30-60 days for customers in India and 30-120 days for overseas customers.  The Group’s customers primarily consist of 
Original Equipment Manufacturers (“OEM”) for its primary products and Dealers for spare parts.
  The Group assesses the credit risk of its customers and dealers at the time of acceptance of the customer as well as on an 
ongoing basis. Before accepting any new customer, the Group uses an external/internal credit scoring system to assess the 
potential customer’s credit quality and defines credit limits by customer. The credit limit of these customers and dealers is 
continuously monitored and recalibrated based on the credit risk assessment.  Most of the OEM’s have high credit ratings 
which helps the Group mitigate credit risk.
  The Group assesses at each reporting date whether a trade receivable or a group of trade receivables is impaired.  The 
Group recognises lifetime expected credit losses for all trade receivables that do not constitute a financing transaction 
and which are due for more than six months.  The expected credit losses are measured at an amount equal to 12 months 
expected credit losses or at an amount equal to the lifetime expected credit losses if the credit risk on the financial asset 
has increased significantly since initial recognition. The Group uses a practical expedient by computing the expected credit 
loss allowance for trade receivables based on a provision matrix.

  Investments consist mainly of investments in mutual funds, insurance premium and short term funds. Other financial assets 
consist of Government incentives receivable, export incentives and security deposits for business purposes.
  Investments in mutual funds are primarily those instruments which have been approved by the management and are in 
low-risk category and are continuously monitored by the management. The Group considers credit risk in investments as 
well as in other financial assets to be very low.
 ii) Liquidity Risk 
  Liquidity risk is the risk that the Group may not be in a position to meet its financial liabilities.  The objective of liquidity 
risk management is to maintain sufficient liquidity and to ensure availability of adequate funds for business.  The Group 
generates sufficient internal accruals and generally the purpose of borrowings is to meet temporary fund flow mismatches 
and to meet regular capital expenditures. The Group maintains a very low debt to equity ratio. 
  The maturity profile of various financial liabilities is as given below. These amounts have been drawn up based on the 
undiscounted cash flows of various financial liabilities based on the earliest date on which the Group can be required to pay.
 iii) Market Risk 
  Market risk is the risk that the fair value of future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes 
in market prices.  Market risk comprises three types of risk: interest rate risk, currency risk and other price risk like 
commodity prices risk. 
  1) Interest rate risk
   Interest rate risk is the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of 
changes in market interest rates. The Group’s exposure to the risk of changes in market interest rates relates primarily 
to the Group’s debt obligations which have floating rate indebtedness.  The Group also maintain deposits of cash and 
cash equivalents with banks and other financial institutions which are subject to periodic resets.

  3) Commodity Price Risk
   The Group is exposed to risks in fluctuation of prices of certain raw materials, which are used as key inputs in the 
production process, especially ferrous and non-ferrous metals.  Historically, as a practice, and as per our understanding 
with customers, the Group has passed on an increase in the cost of metals, especially aluminium and steel to its 
customers and does not foresee a significant risk to its statement of profit and loss on account of fluctuations in the 
prices of materials.
   The Group is further exposed to risks in fluctuation of certain costs of production. It hedges a part of these risks by 
using commodities swap instruments in line with its risk management policies. Refer sub note 4 below.
  4) Derivative financial instruments :
   The Group has entered into foreign currency forward contracts, interest rate swaps and commodity swaps to manage 
its exposure to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates, interest rates and commodity price risk. The counterparty is 
generally a bank. These financial exposures are managed in accordance with the Group's risk management policies 
and procedures. The information on derivative instruments is as follows:

36 Government incentives :
a) Industrial Promotion Subsidy:
 The Company recognises grant income under the Package Scheme of Incentives, Government of Maharashtra (“PSI Scheme”) 
on sale of goods, as management believes that the realisation of the grant income is reasonably certain.
 Incentive under Mega Project Scheme - PSI 2019 (Refer note 18.01)
 The Company has recognized an amount of H 110.10 crore (previous year H 38.13 crore ) as grant income under Mega Project 
scheme PSI 2019 for the year ended 31st March, 2026.
 Incentive under Mega Project Scheme - PSI 2013 (Refer note 18.01)

 (i) Hero Electric Vehicles Private Limited (‘Hero Electric’)
  During the previous year, pursuant to a petition filed by one of the operational creditor of Hero Electric under the Insolvency 
and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (‘Code’), the Hon’ble National Company Law Tribunal (‘NCLT’), New Delhi bench, vide its 
order dated 20th December 2024, admitted Hero Electric into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (‘CIRP’) and has 
appointed the Interim Resolution Professional (‘IRP’) for conducting the CIRP as per the code.
  During the previous financial year, the company has made a provision for expected credit loss of trade receivables of  
H 1.42 crore and classified as an exceptional item.
  During the current financial year, the Hon’ble National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi bench, vide its order dated 3rd 
March 2026, has ordered the liquidation of Hero Electric under Section 33 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 
following the failure of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) to approve a resolution plan. 
  In view of the liquidation proceedings and the low probability of recovery from the liquidation estate, the Company has 
reversed the existing provision for expected credit loss amounting to H 1.42 crore and recorded a write-off for bad debts 
amounting to H 1.42 crore which is disclosed in Note no. 23 ‘Other expenses’.

INDEPENDENT ASSURANCE 
STATEMENT 
Independent Assurance Statement to Endurance Technologies Limited on its BRSR Core Indicators for FY 2025-26
The Board of Directors, 
Endurance Technologies Limited,  
E-92, M.I.D.C Industrial Area, 
Waluj, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar- 431 136 
Maharashtra, India. 
Nature of the Assurance 
SGS India Private Limited (hereinafter referred to as ‘SGS 
India’) was engaged by Endurance Technologies Limited 
(the ‘Company’) to conduct an independent assurance of the 
Company’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting 
(BRSR) (the ‘Core Report’) for the reporting period of April 1, 
2025, to March 31, 2026. SGS India has conducted a Reasonable 
level of Assurance for the BRSR core indicators. This assurance 
engagement was conducted in accordance with International 
Standard on Assurance Engagements (ISAE) 3000 (Revised) 
and ISAE 3410. 
Reporting Framework 
The Report has been prepared following 
1. Master Circular for compliance with the provisions of the 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 by 
listed entities: BRSR Core and Non-Core Framework for 
Assurance and ESG Disclosures for Value Chain (Circular 
No. HO/49/14/14(7)2025-CFD-POD2/I/3762/2026), dated 
30 January 2026.
2. Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and 
Reporting Standard.
Intended Users of this Assurance Statement 
This Assurance Statement is provided with the intention of 
informing all Endurance Technologies Limited internal and 
external Stakeholders.  
Responsibilities 
The information in the report and its presentation are the 
responsibility of the Company’s management. SGS India has not 
been involved in the preparation of any of the material included 
in the report. 
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the text, data, 
and statements within the defined scope of assurance, aiming 
to inform the management of the Company, and in alignment 
with the agreed terms of reference. We do not accept or assume 
any responsibility beyond this specific scope. The Statement shall not be used for interpreting the overall performance of 
the Company, except for the aspects explicitly mentioned 
within the scope. 
Assurance Standard 
SGS has conducted a Reasonable level of Assurance for 
BRSR core parameters under 9 ESG Attributes, including 
essential indicators as specified under BRSR core standards 
and amendments made as on date. This engagement was 
performed in accordance with the International Standard on 
Assurance Engagement (ISAE) 3000 (revised) and ISAE 3410 
(Assurance Engagements other than Audits or Reviews of 
Historical Financial Information). 
Our evidence-gathering procedures were designed to obtain a 
‘Reasonable’ level of assurance, which is a high level of assurance 
in accordance with ISAE 3000 (revised) standard, but is not 
absolute certainty. It involves obtaining sufficient appropriate 
evidence to support the conclusion that the information 
presented in the report is fairly stated and is free from material 
misstatements. 
Statement of Independence and Competence 
The SGS Group of companies is the world leader in inspection, 
testing, and assurance, operating in more than 140 countries and 
providing services including management systems and service 
certification; quality, environmental, social, and ethical auditing 
and training; and environmental, social, and sustainability report 
assurance. SGS India affirms our independence from Endurance 
Technologies Limited, being free from bias and conflicts of 
interest with the organization, its subsidiaries, and stakeholders.  
The assurance team was assembled based on their knowledge, 
experience, and qualifications for this assignment, and 
comprised auditors registered with ISO 26000, ISO 20121, ISO 
50001, SA8000, RBA, QMS, EMS, SMS, GPMS, CFP , WFP , GHG 
Verification, and GHG Validation Lead Auditors, and experience 
on the SRA Assurance. 
Scope of Assurance 
The assurance process involved assessing the quality, accuracy, 
and reliability of BRSR Indicators (KPIs) within the report for the 
period April 1, 2025, to March 31, 2026. The reporting scope and

|Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting01-70

boundaries include 20 sites, 1 office, and 5 R&D centers spread 
across different states in India.  
Assurance Methodology 
The assurance comprised a combination of desktop review, 
interaction with the key personnel engaged in the process of 
developing the report, on-site visits, and remote verification of 
data. Specifically, SGS India undertook the following activities:
	 Assessment of the suitability of the applicable criteria in 
terms of their comprehensiveness, reliability, and accuracy.
	 Interaction with key personnel responsible for collecting, 
consolidating, and calculating the BRSR core and essential 
indicators, and assessing the internal control mechanisms 
in place to ensure data quality.
	 Application of analytical procedures and verification of 
documents on a sample basis for the compilation and 
reporting of the KPIs.
	 Assessing the aggregation process of data at the 
Head Office level.
	 Critical review of the report regarding the plausibility and 
consistency of qualitative and quantitative information 
related to the KPIs.
Limitations 
SGS India did not come across any limitation to the agreed 
scope of the assurance engagement. SGS India verified data on a sample basis; the responsibility for the authenticity of 
the data entirely lies with the Company. The assurance scope 
excluded forward-looking statements, product- or service-
related information, external information sources, and expert 
opinions. SGS India has not been involved in the evaluation or 
assessment of any financial data/performance of the company. 
Our opinion on financial indicators is based on the third-party 
financial reports audited by the Company. SGS India does not 
take any responsibility for the financial data reported in the 
audited financial reports of the Company. 
The assurance scope excludes:
	 Disclosures other than those mentioned in the 
assurance scope.
	 Data reviews outside the operational sites as mentioned in 
the reporting boundary.
	 Validation of any data and information other than those 
presented in “Findings and Conclusions”.
	 The assurance engagement considers an uncertainty of 
±5% based on the materiality threshold for Assumption/
estimation/measurement errors and omissions.
	 The Company’s statements that describe the expression 
of opinion, belief, aspiration, expectation, aim to future 
intention provided by the Company, and assertions related 
to Intellectual Property Rights and other competitive issues.
	 Mapping of the Report with reporting frameworks other 
than those mentioned in the Reporting Criteria above.

Based on the procedures we have performed and the evidence we have obtained, we are satisfied that the information presented by 
the Company in its report (as per the table below) is complete, accurate, reliable, fairly stated in all material respects, and is prepared

 c. A brief on the type of customers 
  Endurance Technologies Limited serves leading Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) across the two, three and 
four-wheeler segments in both domestic and international markets. A complete solutions provider, the Company offers a 
comprehensive range of products across aluminium die-casting, suspension, braking systems, transmission, and embedded 
electronics for these vehicle segments. The Company has also expanded its offerings to address the non-automotive 
segment, including aluminium castings for generator applications, solar dampers and actuators and lithium-ion battery 
packs to cater for telecom, battery energy storage systems, and inverters. The Company’s Aftermarket business addresses 
retail demand in India and select export markets, offering suspension, transmission, braking systems, and other value-
added products through a wide network of distributors.

1. Environmental 
Impacts 
(Climate, 
Energy, Waste)Risk Environmental impacts, 
particularly relating to climate 
change, energy consumption, 
and waste management, can have 
direct and indirect implications 
on operational efficiency, 
cost structures, regulatory 
compliance, and long-term 
business sustainability. Increasing 
regulatory requirements 
(emission norms, waste 
management rules, and potential 
carbon pricing) and oversight 
from the Pollution Control Boards 
increase compliance risk.
Additionally, customers, investors, 
and OEMs (including those with 
global supply chain linkages) 
are increasingly prioritising low-
carbon and resource-efficient 
operations. Inability to align with 
these expectations may impact 
competitiveness and business 
continuity.A structured sustainability roadmap, with defined 
goals and milestones, guides the Company’s 
transition towards more sustainable operations. This is 
supported by strong governance, including oversight 
by top management, robust monitoring mechanisms, 
and structured rewards and recognition. Employee 
engagement and involvement in driving the overall 
sustainability agenda is achieved through training, 
sustainability workshops, and innovation programmes.
The Company complies with applicable environmental 
regulations on the handling of hazardous and non-
hazardous waste as well as Extended Producer 
Responsibility (EPR). The Company follows the 
principles of Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle (3R) to 
enhance resource efficiency and advance circularity. 
Initiatives such as returnable packaging and coolant 
recycling minimise waste generation. A significant 
portion of aluminium scrap is recycled, contributing 
to an overall recycling rate of over 98%. Zero Waste 
to Landfill (ZWTL) certification has been expanded 
during the year, with the number of certified sites 
increasing from 6 to 14. In addition, over 800 tonnes 
of waste have been redirected to co-processing in 
cement industries.
The Company has a decarbonisation plan and shall 
submit the Net Zero roadmap to SBTi (Science 
Based Targets initiative) for validation. Renewable 
energy sourcing through rooftop solar installations, 
open access solar arrangements, and hybrid wind-
solar solutions remains a key focus area under 
the decarbonisation roadmap. The Company is 
prioritising renewable energy deployment at energy-
intensive locations to improve energy security by 
reducing dependence on conventional grid power 
and supporting long-term reduction in Scope 
2 emissions. Continuous evaluation of captive, 
group captive, and open access renewable energy 
opportunities by location is being undertaken. 
Energy conservation teams across locations enable 
continuous improvement and horizontal deployment 
of best practices. The Company installed fuel fitch 
and magnetic resonators for thermal efficiency. As a 
part of the decarbonisation roadmap, the Company 
continued its transition to cleaner fuels like Piped 
Natural Gas (PNG). There was focused adoption 
of technologies such as waste heat recovery, heat 
pumps, high-efficiency compressors, energy-efficient 
motors and equipment, and fuel optimisation to 
reduce energy intensity. Other initiatives include 
power efficiency upgrades and fuel optimisation using 
magnetic resonators for improved combustion.Positive and 
Negative
Opportunity Focused action on climate, 
energy, and waste can unlock 
efficiency gains, reduce 
operating costs, and improve 
margin resilience, particularly 
in energy-intensive processes. 
Transition towards cleaner energy 
and optimised resource use can 
also reduce exposure to future 
regulatory and carbon-related 
costs.
Strengthening environmental 
performance supports alignment 
with evolving OEM and investor 
expectations, enabling deeper 
integration into value chains 
and enhancing long-term 
competitiveness.

The Company is driving climate action by undertaking 
lifecycle assessments for its products to identify priority 
environmental impacts (‘hotspots’) across the product 
lifecycle. This has led to the development of action 
plans across the value chain, including increasing 
the use of recycled metal content, localisation of 
suppliers, supply chain optimisation, process redesign 
for yield improvement, etc. In addition, the innovation 
team, in collaboration with OEMs, has developed 
lightweighting solutions across products, contributing 
to the reduction of Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions 
in the use phase. Other supplier-focused initiatives are 
discussed under the topic Sustainable Supply Chain.
For more details, refer to Principle 6, Essential

2. Environmental 
Impact (Air, 
Water) Risk Emissions and effluents arising 
from manufacturing activities can 
adversely impact public health 
and surrounding ecosystems. 
Inadequate control and 
monitoring may lead to regulatory 
risks related to environmental 
compliance, resulting in 
operational disruptions, financial 
liabilities, and may impact the 
Company’s social license to 
operate.
The Company’s facility at 
Narsapura is located in a water-
stressed region, as per CGWA 
classification, making water 
availability a key operational risk. 
Increasing demand for water 
across industrial and domestic 
sectors further intensifies this risk. 
Managing water use efficiently, 
along with potential cost 
escalations, is therefore critical to 
ensure business continuity.The Company complies with applicable environmental 
regulations relating to air emissions and wastewater 
management. Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) and 
Effluent Treatment Plant (ETP) systems are deployed 
across its plants to ensure wastewater is treated within 
prescribed limits, with Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) 
systems implemented at relevant locations.
Air emissions are regularly monitored to ensure 
compliance and drive improvement. During the year, 
there was a reduction in Air Emissions by shifting to 
PNG, which is a cleaner fuel. During the year, there 
was electrification of the pre-treatment process across 
all plants, focused on the reduction of SOx, NOx and 
particulate matter (PM). The Company is opting for 
induction furnaces over fuel-based furnaces, which are 
helping reduce air emissions as well as GHG emissions. 
Retrofit Emission Control Devices (RECD) have been 
installed on generator sets, besides other pollution 
control devices such as scrubbers and dust collectors, to 
reduce particulate matter and fugitive emissions. 
The Company focuses on strengthening water 
management and resilience against water scarcity. Water 
consumption is monitored and optimised through defined 
systems and protocols. Recycling and reuse practices are 
implemented across cooling towers, domestic usage, and 
drip irrigation systems to improve efficiency. A water balance 
assessment is in place across plants and is periodically 
reviewed, with actions taken based on the findings. Water 
reduction campaigns were conducted twice during the 
year. Conservation measures include closed-loop water 
curtain systems in paint shops and cascading rinse systems 
in surface treatment processes. These efforts have enabled 
two plants to achieve water-positive status and a reduction 
in water intensity across other locations, including the 
Narsapura plant, which is in a water-stress zone.  
For more details on initiatives, refer to the 
“Sustainability” section in the Annual Report on  
Page 52, Principle 6, Essential Indicators 5 (Water) and 8 
(Air Emissions) and Leadership Indicator 4. Performance 
details are available in Principle 6. 
The Company has also expanded rainwater harvesting and 
undertaken Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives 
to enhance water resilience in surrounding communities. For 
more details on CSR initiatives, refer to the “Corporate Social 
Responsibility” section in the Annual Report on Page 46.Negative

3. Customer 
Focus & 
Innovation Opportunity Fostering strong, collaborative 
relationships with customers 
enables organisations to respond 
swiftly to shifting market dynamics 
and evolving expectations.
Leveraging innovation further 
strengthens agility, supports 
product differentiation, and 
enables the creation of tailored 
solutions, thereby helping 
offer a more compelling value 
proposition. Investment in 
Research and Development 
(R&D) resources, including 
the enabling infrastructure, 
contributes to diversified revenue 
streams, stronger competitive 
positioning, and sustained long-
term growth.The Company places strong emphasis on customer focus 
and innovation, with a clear focus on understanding and 
responding to current and evolving customer needs. This 
is supported through structured customer engagement 
and feedback mechanisms, and guides decision-
making across operations, product development, and 
innovation. Customer satisfaction is driven through a 
focus on Quality, Cost, Delivery, Development, and 
Management (QCDDM), along with product Value 
Analysis and Value Engineering (VAVE), digital tools, and 
process automation. The Quality Management System 
(QMS) integrates customer-specific requirements into 
standardised processes across all plants, supported by 
regular training and audits at system, process, and product 
levels. Customer complaints are addressed through 
structured root cause analysis by cross-functional teams. 
Customer Centricity as a value extends to the aftermarket 
business. The Company has implemented pre-dispatch 
inspections to reduce product returns and added new 
products based on dealer feedback. Various initiatives for 
retailer and mechanic engagement, including training, 
canopy events, etc., are conducted. The Company has 
also enhanced its Endurance Saathi App as a feedback 
mechanism for the retailers and mechanics who purchase 
the Company’s products from its dealers. This enables 
self-registration, product search and ordering based 
on availability across distributors as well as instant 
payouts for the Company’s loyalty program. The App 
includes a referral feature, marketing materials, a tiered 
performance and rewards program with a leaderboard to 
embed gamification into the program.  
The Company’s R&D efforts build on this approach, 
focusing on strengthening technology capabilities while 
delivering cost-effective and sustainable solutions. 
Through global collaborations, it continues to enhance 
capabilities across product segments, with several projects 
under development that are expected to evolve into 
global platforms—manufactured in India and supplied to 
international markets. Key focus areas include specialised 
material development to improve durability, maintain 
performance under extreme conditions, and develop 
robust, abuse-resistant systems. The Company is also 
transitioning towards simulation-driven development to 
improve design accuracy, reduce development cycles, 
and enhance efficiency. These initiatives are supported 
by sustained investments in R&D infrastructure, with 
significant investment during the year to strengthen in-
house testing and development capabilities.Positive
Innovation is encouraged through structured platforms 
that enable employees to contribute ideas, supported by 
Intellectual Property (IP)-focused workshops, recognition 
programmes, and internal policies. During FY2025–26, 
the Company filed 43 patent applications and received 
2 grants, taking the total to 93 granted patents. It also 
filed 39 design registrations and received 20 design 
grants. Participation remained strong, with 75 employees 
contributing to innovation initiatives during the year.
For more details, refer to the Annual Report section 
titled “Research and Development”, on Page 30 
and Page 96 in the ‘Technology Absorption’ section, 
Annexure I to the Board’s Report.

4. Sustainable 
Supply Chain Opportunity By embedding sustainable 
practices throughout its value 
chain, the Company can lower 
its environmental impact while 
strengthening its social impact 
and commitment to being a 
responsible business. Building a 
sustainable supply chain is aligned 
with the Company’s Environment, 
Social and Governance (ESG) 
strategy, Charter, as well as the 
expectations of customers and 
investors. Proactively managing 
ESG-related risks across the 
value chain also creates strategic 
advantages through increased 
resilience of the business model 
while mitigating exposure to 
environmental and social risks. The Company has a Sustainable Sourcing Policy and 
a Vendor Code of Conduct (VCoC), which sets out 
its expectations for suppliers. These are supported 
by well-defined sustainable sourcing procedures and 
robust supplier assessment processes covering health 
and safety, human rights, and environmental risks. The 
Company also undertakes various training sessions 
covering quality, ESG sensitisation and best practices, as 
well as climate-focused workshops. Capability-building 
programmes are conducted to encourage suppliers 
to obtain certifications such as ISO 14001, ISO 45001, 
and GreenCo. Suppliers are further supported through 
Company-led sustainability programmes, including net-
zero training sessions facilitated by industry experts. For 
more details, refer to Principle 1, Leadership Indicator 1 
and Principle 2, Essential Indicator 2.
The Company maintains consistent and meaningful 
engagement with its supplier network, recognising 
collaboration as central to advancing its sustainability 
agenda. The Endurance Vendor Association (EVA) 
serves as a key platform for regular dialogue, 
addressing concerns and sharing knowledge on ESG 
best practices. It enables suppliers to support the 
Company’s environmental and social commitments 
while also providing a structured feedback mechanism 
for continuous improvement. The growing participation 
in EVA reflects a strengthening collective commitment 
to responsible and collaborative business practices. 
The Company also recognises exceptional supplier 
performance across a range of categories, including 
quality, ESG, and technology upgradation, with 43 
suppliers receiving awards across 10 categories during 
the reporting year.
The Company has defined a sustainability index to track 
the ESG performance of critical suppliers, while supplier 
performance more broadly is monitored through ESG 
audits, supplier system and capabilities reviews, and 
third-party assessments, with focused corrective action 
plans being tracked for closure. Suppliers relevant for 
BRSR Core value chain reporting have been identified 
and trained to align with these requirements, ensuring 
a standardised approach across the supply chain. In 
addition, the digitalisation of supplier quality processes 
enables timely and transparent communication, 
supporting a more efficient supply chain. The Company 
adopts a strategic approach to supplier development by 
identifying long-term and critical suppliers and actively 
supporting them in building their capabilities, while 
embedding sustainability criteria into procurement 
evaluations to support Scope 3 GHG alignment, 
responsible sourcing, and overall value chain resilience.

5. Health & 
Safety Risk ‘Health and Safety’ is critical to 
operational effectiveness, as gaps 
can lead to workplace incidents, 
regulatory non-compliance, 
production disruptions, and 
reputational impact. Inadequate 
safety practices may also affect 
workforce morale, increase 
absenteeism, and reduce 
productivity, thereby impacting 
overall business performance. 
Failure to comply with applicable 
health and safety regulations can 
result in regulatory action and 
financial penalties. Ensuring a safe 
and healthy work environment is 
therefore essential for business 
continuity and maintaining 
stakeholder confidence.The Company is committed to providing a safe and healthy 
workplace for employees, workers, and on-site personnel, 
with a zero-tolerance approach to unsafe practices. Health 
and safety are key management priorities, with safety 
performance reviewed regularly by the Managing Director 
and senior management through periodic and cross-
functional reviews. The Board also periodically reviews 
the Company’s progress and performance on Health and 
Safety. The Occupational Health and Safety Management 
System (OHSMS) is implemented across plants to identify 
and manage workplace risks, aligned with the “Safety 
First, Zero Harm” approach.
Key measures include strong infrastructure and 
operational controls, regular safety training, and strict 
adherence to personal protective equipment (PPE) 
protocols. During the year, the Company strengthened 
its safety practices through initiatives such as Visual 
Safety Leadership (VSL), appointment of Safety 
Champions across departments, and deployment 
of Night Duty Officers to enhance monitoring and 
employee engagement. The Company has also 
established a comprehensive health and wellness 
ecosystem to support the physical, mental, emotional, 
and financial well-being of employees and their 
families through a hybrid model, with targeted 
interventions such as annual health check-ups, women-
specific programmes, milestone-based recognition, 
and “Know Your Policy” sessions.
For more details, refer to Principle 3, Essential 
Indicators 10 and 12.Negative
6. Labour 
ManagementRisk Strong labour relations are critical 
to maintain stable operations and 
a conducive work environment. 
Ineffective management of 
labour relations may lead to 
disruptions in operations, 
reduced productivity, compliance 
gaps, and potential legal or 
regulatory issues arising from 
disputes, along with reputational 
impact and stakeholder concerns.The Company’s workforce comprises both permanent 
and contractual workers, supported by dedicated 
industrial relations teams at each plant. Clear policies 
are in place covering wages, health and safety, human 
rights, grievance redressal, and collective bargaining. 
Workers are provided with medical and insurance 
coverage, while contractual workers are supported 
in accessing benefits such as the Employees’ State 
Insurance Corporation (ESIC), Labour Welfare Fund 
(LWF), and other applicable schemes. Additional 
support includes performance-linked incentives such 
as attendance bonuses, heat allowance, productivity 
incentives, and rejoining bonuses. Subsidised meals 
are provided across plants through canteen facilities.
The Company has established multiple engagement 
mechanisms to support workforce participation and 
motivation. Initiatives such as the On-the-Spot Award 
programme recognise performance, while the ‘Mitra’ 
Buddy Programme supports new joiners in workplace 
integration. Regular medical camps and wellness 
sessions promote employee health, and team-building 
activities strengthen collaboration. The Company also 
invests in skill development through the Learn, Earn, 
Grow & Success (LEGS) programme, a three-year 
diploma in Manufacturing Technology conducted in 
partnership with Nettur Technical Training Foundation 
(NTTF), providing on-the-job training for 12th pass-out 
students. Worker feedback is actively sought through 
structured channels, with actions taken based on 
inputs received. These efforts support a stable work 
environment and help minimise the risk of disruptions.
Labour management is anchored in the principles of 
human capital development; for more information, 
please refer to the “Human Resource” section of the 
Annual Report on Page 40.Negative

7. Employee 
ExperienceOpportunity A supportive and inclusive 
workplace helps maintain 
productivity, protect knowledge 
within the organisation, and 
strengthen the Company’s

The Company aims to be an

Competence, Career, and Connect—guides its people 
strategy and is supported by a dedicated HR team and 
defined policies focused on employee development, 
well-being, engagement, and inclusion. A structured 
grievance redressal mechanism, managed by a 
dedicated committee, ensures the timely resolution of 
employee concerns. 
Employee well-being is driven through a variety of 
health and medical insurance coverage (with a term 
life insurance being added in the reporting year), 
as well as access to non-occupational healthcare 
services. Wellness webinars, self-care sessions, and 
organisation-wide initiatives such as Fitness Challenge 
and Wellness Month are conducted regularly. 
Employee engagement is enabled through platforms 
such as ‘Hi-Five with HR’, Infinity Bridge, Leadedge, 
and leadership connect sessions, along with family 
connect programmes, hobby groups, and cultural and 
festive events. Idea-generation is encouraged through 
initiatives such as Shark Tank, Kaizen, and suggestion 
schemes. Recognition and feedback are embedded 
through tools such as the Net Promoter Score (NPS) 
survey and the WOW Rewards & Recognition Portal, 
supported by initiatives like Appreciation Week. 
Employee participation has increased by 30%-40% 
across various engagement initiatives, and the culture 
of recognition has led to increased adoption of the 
WOW platform. A key indicator of the success of 
the employee experience approach is evidenced by 
the growing participation in the NPS surveys and the 
consistent improvement in the scores over the past 3 
years.
Capability building is driven through structured 
learning and development programmes, including 
the Endurance Leadership Academy (ELA), Endurance 
Talent Advancement Programme (E-TAP), ‘RISE’ (a 
plant head Qualification Program), the HR Edge 
Program, and SAMVEDANA, a six-month coaching-
led programme for Zonal, Regional, and Area Sales 
Managers. These initiatives aim to strengthen 
leadership depth, build a robust leadership 
pipeline, and support career progression across the 
organisation. Over 150 mid-level managers have 
completed ELA, while 15 leaders are currently part of 
the RISE programme to develop future Plant Heads 
and strengthen a future-ready workforce.

8. Diversity Opportunity Embracing diversity fuels 
innovation and sparks creativity by 
combining various perspectives 
and experiences. A diverse 
workforce is more adept at 
understanding and meeting the 
needs of a broad customer base, 
which leads to better products 
and services. Inclusive workplaces 
attract top-tier talent and boost 
reputation and employee morale. 
When leadership reflects a variety 
of backgrounds, decision-making 
and problem-solving become 
more dynamic and effective. 
Teams made up of individuals 
with different viewpoints tend to 
be more productive, delivering 
stronger results through their 
unique insights and collaborative 
approaches.Diversity at the Company is viewed holistically and 
includes representation across gender, age, regional 
diversity, and persons with disabilities, among other 
dimensions. The Company is committed to advancing 
diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) through structured 
interventions and strong governance frameworks. The 
DEI agenda is guided by the Equal Employer Policy 
and overseen by the Endurance Diversity, Equity, and 
Inclusion Committee (EDEIC). DEI is also embedded 
as a Key Responsibility Area (KRA) in the Balanced 
Scorecard (BSC), ensuring accountability across the 
organisation. There are well-defined policies covering 
the safety and security of women at the workplace, and 
Prevention of Sexual Harassment (POSH) awareness 
programmes are conducted regularly to maintain a 
respectful workplace environment. 
Key initiatives such as Diversity Week and the “Winning 
with Women” platform are undertaken to drive 
awareness and employee engagement. Additionally, 
women-focused interventions, including self-defence 
programmes and health and hygiene workshops, are 
conducted to support women’s safety and well-being. 
Capability-building is strengthened through web-based 
DEI training modules and unconscious bias workshops 
for leaders, enabling inclusive leadership and decision-
making.
The Company has made measurable progress in 
improving gender diversity at leadership levels. Focused 
hiring initiatives such as the ‘SHE Endurance Drive’ and 
the Diversity Referral Program continue to enhance 
female participation. During recruitment, preference 
is given to female candidates where capabilities are 
comparable. Tailored development programmes 
under the Endurance Leadership Academy support the 
creation of a diverse and future-ready talent pipeline 
with over 100 female employees above entry level 
being groomed for mid-senior roles. The Company 
has also enabled the deployment of female workers on 
evening and night shifts with appropriate safeguards. 
These efforts have resulted in an entire production line 
at one of the Pune plants being operated by female 
workers, including contractual workers.
Collectively, these initiatives contribute to building 
a safe, inclusive, and equitable workplace. They also 
strengthen diversity across levels and enable long-term 
organisational resilience.

9. Human Rights Risk Non-adherence to human rights 
standards across the Company’s 
operations or supply chain 
can lead to legal challenges, 
financial penalties, and employee 
dissatisfaction. Such issues 
may disrupt productivity, harm 
the Company’s reputation and 
weaken consumer confidence, 
potentially affecting sales 
performance. In addition, 
labour disputes or allegations 
such as child labour can cause 
operational delays, increase 
costs, and impact the overall 
efficiency and reliability of the 
supply chain.The Company is committed to respecting and 
upholding human rights across its operations and 
value chain. The Company emphasises fair wages, 
supports freedom of association, and ensures 
adherence to all applicable legal and regulatory 
requirements. It maintains a zero-tolerance approach 
to discrimination, child labour, and forced labour, 
and has established robust mechanisms for the 
prevention of sexual harassment at the workplace. 
POSH sensitisation is conducted for all employees and 
workers at the induction phase and reinforced through 
classroom training. The Endurance Code of Conduct 
(ECOC) also lays down guidelines related to various 
Human Rights aspects. 
This commitment is reinforced through a structured 
audit protocol for statutory compliance by contract 
worker providers, as detailed in Principle 3, Leadership 
Indicator 2. The contract labour management system 
(CLMS) is linked to the contract workers’ Aadhar cards 
to ensure compliance with child labour regulations. 
Human rights principles are integrated into contractual 
agreements with contractors, vendors, and suppliers, 
ensuring accountability across the supply chain. 
Further periodic assessment of suppliers is conducted 
to monitor adherence to Human Rights requirements 
embodied in the VCOC.

12. Information

Data PrivacyRisk Inadequate protection of 
data and intellectual property 
can expose the Company to

compromising the confidentiality 
of sensitive information.Cybersecurity risks are proactively managed, and data 
privacy obligations are upheld through the Company’s 
robust and mature Information Security Management 
System (ISMS). The Company continues to align its 
information security governance with ISO 27001:2022 
standards, with independent re-certification and 
periodic assessments conducted. The Company has 
also achieved Trusted Information Security Assessment 
Exchange (TISAX) Level 3 accreditation. The framework 
is further strengthened through the enablement of 
Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA), enhanced Security 
Operations Centre (SOC) capabilities for continuous 
monitoring and rapid threat response, and improved 
hardening of network and operating systems to reduce 
vulnerabilities. The Company continues to maintain 
a strong track record in safeguarding customer data 
privacy and cybersecurity. The effectiveness of this 
framework was demonstrated during an incident, where 
core systems remained secure, no customer data was 
compromised, and operations were restored within 
defined timelines without any material business impact.

Indicator 5.Negative

disruptions, energy market volatility and evolving transition requirements. 
During the year, we continued to advance the priorities under our ESG 2030 
Roadmap while strengthening the integration of sustainability considerations 
into capital allocations, operational and business decision-making. 
Our focus remained on decarbonisation, resource efficiency and circularity 
across operations. We progressed on our Science Based Targets initiative 
(SBTi) commitment, while three plants achieved the CII GreenCo Gold 
rating, reflecting continued improvements in environmental performance 
and sustainable manufacturing practices. We also accelerated initiatives 
relating to renewable energy adoption, water stewardship, waste 
recycling and afforestation to strengthen long-term operational resilience 
while supporting growth through sustainable practices.
We also continued to strengthen our focus on customer-centric innovation 
through sustained emphasis on customer focus, quality, Value Analysis 
and Value Engineering engagements, and technology-led product 
development. Investments in R&D, advanced engineering capabilities and 
simulation-driven development supported the delivery of high-quality, 
cost-effective and sustainable solutions aligned with evolving customer 
requirements. These efforts remain closely aligned with the Company’s 
long-term business strategy, competitiveness and growth ambitions across 
domestic and global markets. We deepened our engagement across 
our supply chain in line with the BRSR Core framework and our Net-Zero 
ambitions. During the year, we worked closely with suppliers on emissions 
reporting, decarbonisation planning and responsible business practices, 
while progressively embedding ESG considerations into procurement 
through supplier assessments, audits and capability-building initiatives. 
The Endurance Vendor Association (EVA) is a strong example of our 
collaborative approach towards sustainable value chain development.
On the social front, we continued to prioritise health, safety and employee 
well-being through robust systems, structured training programmes and 
leadership oversight across operations. Building a competence-driven 
culture and engaged workforce is crucial for our continued performance, 
and our employee NPS reflects this emphasis. We also strengthened 
digital systems across stakeholder engagement mechanisms, operational 
automation for driving better outcomes, and enabling stronger ESG 
monitoring, transparency and assurance readiness. As sustainability 
expectations continue to evolve, we remain focused on building a 
resilient, responsible and future-ready organisation through strong 
governance, accountable leadership and disciplined execution, aligned 
with long-term stakeholder value creation.”

Yes, the Company has implemented an Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bribery Policy that reinforces its commitment to the highest 
standards of integrity, transparency, and ethical conduct. The Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bribery Policy is available on the Company’s 
website at https://www.endurancegroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/anti-corruption-and-anti-bribery-policy.pdf.
The aforesaid Policy underscores the Company’s zero-tolerance approach to bribery and corruption in any form, including 
the offering, promising, giving, or accepting of improper payments or benefits with the intent of securing an unfair business 
advantage. It sets out specific prohibitions, reporting processes, and defined compliance obligations to promote consistent 
adherence across all levels of the organisation. The said Policy applies to all directors, employees, trainees, and third parties 
representing or acting on behalf of the Company, including agents, contractors, and consultants. Any suspected instances 
of violation are required to be reported in accordance with the Vigil Mechanism-cum-Whistleblower Policy of the Company. 
Additionally, the Company’s zero-tolerance commitment toward bribery and corruption is also reflected in the Code of Conduct 
for Employees (ECOC). Appropriate training and awareness sessions are carried out for internal as well as external stakeholders 
on these policies and reporting mechanisms. ECOC is available on the Company’s website at https://www.endurancegroup.

2. Does the entity have processes in place to avoid / manage conflicts of interest involving members of the Board? (Yes / 
No). If yes, provide details of the same. 
 Yes, to ensure that the Company’s interests are always prioritised, a Code of Conduct for Directors and Senior Management 
Personnel of the Company has been adopted. Conflict of interest can undermine the trust the Company has earned from its 
stakeholders and may damage the reputation it has built over the years. Such conflicts are not always direct and may arise 
through personal, financial, or professional relationships that could influence decision-making. The aforesaid Code therefore 
requires Directors and senior executives to disclose any actual or potential conflicts of interest, including personal interests in 
transactions that may conflict with the Company’s objectives. It also restricts Directors from serving on the board of any competing 
entity without prior approval of the Board, thereby reinforcing transparency, accountability, and effective oversight. Further, 
the Code is in accordance with Regulation 26(5) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015, wherein Directors and senior management are required to disclose all material financial or commercial transactions where 
their personal interests may conflict with those of the Company. The Company obtains these declarations regularly to ensure 
continued compliance, transparency, and responsible governance practices. The said Code can be reviewed at: https://www.
endurancegroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/code-of-conduct-for-directors-and-smp-april-2024-1.pdf. Leadership Indicators

2. a. Does the entity have procedures in place for sustainable sourcing? 
  The Company has laid down a detailed Vendor Code of Conduct (VCOC) that establishes the Company’s expectations 
on environmental, social, and ethical as well as health and safety (EHS) norms. All suppliers provide a self-certification on 
adherence to the VCOC, and this is monitored periodically through a robust assessment framework. 
  The Company has implemented an SQM system that encompasses its sustainable sourcing framework across both direct 
and indirect procurement, and receives a declaration from suppliers confirming adherence to the SQM. The Company 
conducts supplier quality training annually through the Company’s faculty and external experts. A risk-based audit 
approach has been established where supplier criticality and the nature of processes help determine audit frequency and 
the depth of supplier assessments. This enables focused oversight and effective risk management across the supply chain. 
28  
|Endurance Technologies Limited
=== page 299 ===
Additionally, identified suppliers are measured against a comprehensive sustainability index that measures performance 
across a variety of ESG parameters and are required to adhere to defined green sourcing Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). 
To further strengthen supplier capabilities, ETL conducts regular sustainability-focused training programmes, including 
specialised Net Zero sessions delivered in collaboration with CII experts.
  For direct procurement categories (raw materials and components), all new and existing suppliers undergo a structured 
evaluation and audit process. The assessment framework covers a broad range of parameters, including quality and 
process management systems, document control, purchasing and sub-supplier management, material handling, preventive 
maintenance, tooling controls, inspection systems, training, and category-specific requirements. Supplier monitoring 
parameters also include compliance with environmental, legal, and statutory requirements, as well as workplace health 
and safety practices, ensuring alignment with the Company’s sustainability expectations. Suppliers not meeting acceptable 
thresholds are provided time-bound and focused action plans, with defined escalation processes for non-performance. 
Suppliers unable to meet expectations are de-prioritised and may be replaced. In addition, new suppliers are evaluated 
on financial parameters, business continuity, and business ethics during onboarding, and only those meeting defined 
criteria are approved for engagement. For indirect procurement, including fuel, capital goods, and other operational 
inputs, clearly defined specifications, grades, and quality standards are established to ensure responsible sourcing. The 
engagement of contract labour and service providers is governed in accordance with applicable regulations, including 
the Contract Labour Act, ensuring adherence to statutory requirements and responsible employment practices. Supplier 
performance is continuously evaluated, and suppliers demonstrating measurable improvements are recognised through 
structured reward and recognition programmes at vendor meets.
  The Company adopts a strategic approach towards supplier development by identifying long-term and critical suppliers 
within its value chain and actively supporting them in building their capabilities. A detailed capability assessment is 
undertaken across dimensions such as business profile, financial strength, operational performance, customer base, market 
presence, certification status, and supply chain relevance. Based on these insights, targeted interventions—including 
process improvements, quality enhancement initiatives, capacity augmentation, and compliance strengthening—are 
implemented in collaboration with suppliers. During the reporting year, 94 suppliers were assessed, of which 87 were 
deemed “capable” as per the defined scoring criteria.
  The Company engages actively with its suppliers and has established a supplier-run association, called the EVA, to enhance 
collaboration and provide a collective platform to address broader issues. Capability building and best practice sharing 
sessions are conducted periodically to improve supplier awareness on sustainability and operational excellence. Details 
of awareness and training programmes conducted during the year are provided under Principle 1, Leadership Indicator 
1, while additional information on sustainable sourcing and the green supply chain is available on Page 44 of the Annual 
Report in the “Supply Chain” section.
 b. If yes, what percentage of inputs were sourced sustainably? 89.44% 
3. Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling, and disposal at the end of life, for 
(a) Plastics (including packaging) (b) E-waste (c) Hazardous waste, and (d) other waste.
 The Company manufactures auto components and supplies them to OEM customers. As these customers are not the final 
users of the products, the Company does not directly reclaim products at the end of their lifecycle. In accordance with the 
guidelines issued by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), Government of India, OEMs have adopted various 
End-of-Life Vehicle (ELV) strategies to enhance circularity across the vehicle lifecycle. These strategies emphasise circular design 
considerations, the increased use of recycled materials, and ongoing improvements in sustainable packaging. As part of the 
OEM value chain, the Company undertakes value addition and value engineering initiatives that support these principles. 
 For aftermarket products supplied through its dealer networks, the Company follows an exchange policy for parts with 
manufacturing defects, which are subsequently returned to suppliers for recycling and disposal as per stipulated norms. Plastics 
and packaging are managed under the EPR framework, with further details provided under Principle 2, Essential Indicator 4. 
Other waste generated from operations, including E-waste and hazardous waste, is handled in accordance with the disclosures 
provided under Principle 6, Essential Indicator 10.

|Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting01-70

d. Whether Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is applicable to the entity’s activities (Yes / No). If yes, whether the 
waste collection plan is in line with the EPR plan submitted to the Pollution Control Boards? If not, provide steps taken 
to address the same.
 Yes, the Company is registered with the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) as both a “Brand Owner” and an “Importer” 
in alignment with the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, and the EPR Guidelines. EPR obligations for both pre-consumer 
and post-consumer plastic waste are determined based on category-wise targets set by the CPCB on the EPR portal. The 
Company meets its targets in collaboration with CPCB-registered recyclers and ensures compliance with applicable regulatory 
requirements for the collection and channelising of plastic waste through environmentally sound recycling and disposal 
processes.  The Company has also registered as a “Producer” for E-Waste and Battery Waste EPR, and the annual return filings 
have been completed. EPR obligations for e-waste and battery waste will become mandatory after 8 years of annual filings, as 
per CPCB guidelines.
 In FY 2024–25, the Company facilitated the recycling of 842 MT of plastic through authorised recycling vendors, and the 
corresponding certifications have been submitted to the CPCB as part of the annual EPR compliance. For FY 2025–26, the EPR 
obligation stands at 695 MT, which will be fulfilled within the timelines prescribed by the CPCB.
 Waste collection plans for plastic waste are aligned with CPCB requirements, and proactive measures are in place for e-waste 
and battery waste EPR compliance when it becomes applicable.

3. Accessibility of workplaces: 
Are the premises / offices of the entity accessible to differently abled employees and workers, as per the requirements of 
the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016? If not, whether any steps are being taken by the entity in this regard.
 The Company currently does not employ any differently abled employees or workers. However, as an Equal Opportunity 
employer, the Company has partnered with a specialised third-party vendor to support compliance with the Rights of Persons 
with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016. A comprehensive review of all relevant policies and processes has been completed as part 
of this commitment. Based on the findings, the vendor has provided a set of recommendations, which are currently being 
implemented to align our practices with the requirements of the RPwD Act. Additionally, the vendor is supporting accessibility 
audits at select upcoming manufacturing plants to ensure that the infrastructure is fully compliant with the RPwD Act regarding 
workplace accessibility for people with disabilities.
4. Does the entity have an equal opportunity policy as per the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016? If so, provide 
a web-link to the policy: 
 Yes. The Company has adopted an Equal Opportunity Policy that reflects its commitment to providing equal employment 
opportunities, promoting diversity, equity and inclusion, and maintaining a workplace free from discrimination in accordance 
with applicable laws and regulations. The policy is implemented under the oversight of business leaders and functional heads 
and is reinforced through periodic awareness initiatives and employee training programmes. Employment-related decisions, 
including recruitment, promotions, career advancement, and compensation, are based strictly on merit to ensure a fair, 
transparent, and non-discriminatory approach. To ensure awareness and accessibility, the policy is available on the Company’s 
intranet portal and is also introduced to employees during the induction process. The policy can be accessed at: https://www.
endurancegroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/equal-opportunity-employer-policy.pdf. The Company follows a zero-
tolerance approach toward discrimination based on disability, gender, religion, ethnicity, age, race, or sexual orientation. In this 
regard, the ECOC includes provisions addressing discrimination and establishes clear mechanisms for reporting or escalating 
concerns relating to discrimination or misconduct. More details are available at: https://www.endurancegroup.com/wp-content/
uploads/2023/06/ECOC.pdf.
 To further promote an open and inclusive work environment, employees are encouraged to share their views and concerns 
through town hall meetings, suggestion boxes, and an anonymous feedback platform.

10. Health and safety management system:
a. Whether an occupational health and safety management system has been implemented by the entity? (Yes / No). If 
yes, the coverage of such system?
  Yes, a structured Occupational Health and Safety Management System is in place across all locations. ISO 45001:2018 
certified plants have been increased to eleven in the reporting period, and the Company will continue to pursue certifications 
for the rest of the plants in a phased manner. All locations follow the guidelines and principles of the standards. The 
Company focuses on a continued improvement approach to enhance the effectiveness of its practices, and details are 
presented in Principle 3, Essential Indicator 12.

|Endurance Technologies Limited
=== page 307 ===
b. What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by 
the entity?
  The Company’s Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) framework is aligned with ISO 45001:2018 and is 
consistently implemented across all plants. It enables systematic identification and evaluation of workplace hazards arising 
from routine and non-routine activities, ensuring risks are appropriately assessed and managed. To drive standardisation 
and consistency in risk assessment practices, a common HIRA template has been developed and deployed across all 
plants. This is supported by uniform risk rating criteria, structured application of the hierarchy of controls, and defined 
documentation protocols. Cross-functional teams have been trained on these aspects to ensure consistent understanding 
and implementation across operations. This is further reinforced through structured safety practices such as the Work 
Permit System and Health, Safety and Environment (HSE) audits, which strengthen on-ground safety oversight and ensure 
effective control of day-to-day operational risks.
  For non-routine activities, the Company undertakes proactive interventions including Gemba walks / management walk-
arounds, spot inspections, and structured feedback mechanisms to identify emerging risks and gaps in controls. An 
established process for incident communication and sharing of key learnings across locations further enhances transparency, 
awareness, and continuous improvement. Together, these measures enable effective risk mitigation and ensure hazards are 
maintained within acceptable limits, fostering a strong safety culture.
c. Whether you have processes for workers to report work-related hazards and to remove themselves from such risks. 
(Yes / No)
  Yes, the Company has established formal mechanisms for workers to report work-related hazards and to remove themselves 
or others from potential risks. This is enabled through a structured safety reporting platform, supported by the appointment 
of Night Duty Officers to ensure continuous monitoring, especially during night shifts. The Company also fosters a strong 
culture of VSL, wherein leadership actively engages in hazard identification and reinforces safe behaviours. In addition, 
daily toolbox talks and regular supervisor interactions enable proactive identification and reporting of unsafe acts, unsafe 
conditions, and near-miss events. Workers may also directly escalate concerns to Safety Committee representatives or 
EHS Officers. These channels are monitored by trained safety personnel to ensure timely acknowledgement, effective 
resolution, and closure of all reported hazards. 
 d. Do the employees / workers of the entity have access to non-occupational medical and healthcare services? (Yes / No)
The Company provides comprehensive non-occupational medical and healthcare support to employees and their families. 
This includes a Health Benefit Plan offering free doctor consultations, discounted diagnostics, surgical planning support, 
and annual preventive health check-ups. The plan has been further enhanced to include Outpatient Department (OPD) 
benefits, enabling easy access to online consultations, hospital visits, and discounted medical services for employees 
and their families. The Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) supports well-being across physical, mental/emotional, 
social, and financial dimensions and is extended to employees and their immediate family members. Regular preventive 
health check-up camps are conducted across manufacturing units to promote early diagnosis, supported by webinars and 
awareness sessions that encourage healthy lifestyle choices. Employees are also covered under Group Medical Coverage 
(GMC) and Group Personal Accident (GPA) policies, reinforcing health security and overall productivity.
For workers, the Company ensures access to essential healthcare through Occupational Health Centres, regular medical 
camps, and ongoing health and hygiene initiatives, including vaccination drives and heat stress management. Preventive 
care is promoted through sessions on hypertension, diabetes, and lifestyle-related diseases, along with targeted mental 
health support for shift workers and women's wellness initiatives covering physical, mental, emotional, and social well-
being. The Company also organises de-addiction programmes addressing liquor, smoking, and tobacco use to support 
healthier lifestyle choices among workers. To improve awareness and access to statutory benefits, the Company conducts 
programmes with government agencies, including PF and ESIC awareness sessions, Know Your Customer (KYC) camps, 
National Pension Scheme awareness, and Maharashtra Labour Welfare initiatives, while continuing to support workers 
in availing ESIC benefits. Workers are also covered under the Workmen’s Compensation (WC) policy, ensuring financial 
protection in case of workplace contingencies. To promote mental well-being, the Company promotes an engaging work 
environment through birthday and festival celebrations, reward and recognition programmes, indoor and outdoor sports, 
Kaizen competitions, and Women’s Day celebrations.
